title: Remote entanglement need not be the bottleneck for modular trapped-ion quantum computing
authors: Felix W. Knollmann, David P. Nadlinger, John Blue, Sabrina M. Corsetti, Sam J. Bishop, Adam R. Martinez, Jelena Notaros, Colin D. Bruzewicz, Robert McConnell, Isaac L. Chuang
abstract: Modularity underpins classical computing; as quantum processors encounter limits on fabrication yield, reliability, and size, they will need it just as acutely. The bottleneck to linking modules is producing shared entanglement at sufficient rate, density, and fidelity. Trapped ions hold the best demonstrated photonic links, yet they rely on bulky collection optics that cap how densely links can be packed, and their performance trails local gates by two orders of magnitude in rate and fidelity. We synthesize several enabling results $\unicode{x2014}$ single-photon heralding, coherent recoil correction, projective distillation, and trap-integrated photonics $\unicode{x2014}$ into one comprehensive architecture that substantially narrows this gap. Single-photon heralding leads to linear scaling of success probability with detection efficiency, allowing compact integrated photonics to saturate the entanglement rate at a local-operation limit in dense, easy-to-parallelize channels. Addressing its inherent error mechanisms at their source, we project a Bell-pair fidelity of 99.9\% at rates and densities compatible with fault-tolerant operations. Remote entanglement then need not remain the bottleneck for modular trapped-ion computing; the limit shifts to the local operations that must improve regardless.
summary: This paper addresses the scalability challenge in modular trapped-ion quantum computing by tackling the rate and fidelity limitations of remote entanglement links. The authors propose a comprehensive architecture that integrates single-photon heralding with compact photonics and source-level error correction. They conclude that these advancements allow the system to overcome the entanglement bottleneck, suggesting future improvements must focus on local gate operations.
main_problem: The primary challenge is overcoming the bottleneck of generating shared entanglement at a rate, density, and fidelity sufficient for fault-tolerant modular quantum computation.
main_result: By synthesizing single-photon heralding, integrated photonics, and source-level error correction, the authors show that remote entanglement generation can reach rates compatible with local operations, shifting the computational bottleneck elsewhere.
method: The approach involves developing a comprehensive architecture combining advanced quantum optics techniques (single-photon heralding) with physical integration (trap-integrated photonics) and theoretical protocols (projective distillation).
model_or_system: The work focuses on modular trapped-ion Quantum Processing Units (QPUs) linked by 'Bell factories' using surface-electrode ion traps. Entanglement is generated via photonic links connecting these modules.
key_observables: Projected remote Bell-pair rate density ($10^5 	ext{ s}^{-1}	ext{cm}^{-2}$), and achieved fidelity ($\geq 99.9\%$).
important_parameters: Target rates for fault tolerance ($10^4 - 10^6 	ext{ s}^{-1}$ per module); the rate is shown to be limited by the slowest local operation block in a pipeline.
main_assumptions: The argument relies on successfully implementing and synthesizing several mature enabling technologies: single-photon heralding, coherent recoil correction, projective distillation, and compact integrated photonics.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the overall remote entanglement generation architecture. Figure 3 compares heralded entanglement rates for different encoding schemes (e.g., Time-bin vs. Polarization). Figure 4 details the pipelined process flow for generating entangled pairs.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the need for modularity, analyzes current limitations in trapped-ion links compared to local gates, and then proposes a synthesized architecture incorporating multiple advanced techniques (heralding, correction, integration) to overcome the entanglement bottleneck.
why_interesting: It provides a concrete roadmap for scaling quantum processors by addressing the critical interface problem—the reliable, high-rate connection between independently operating quantum modules using established AMO platforms like trapped ions.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Remote entanglement generation architecture. Each quantum processing unit (QPU) is a module consisting of a microfabricated surface-electrode trap with integrated optics. The Bell factory produces and distills remote Bell pairs for intermodule operations. The photonic links consist of single-mode waveguides and fibers. A switch network enables all-to-all connectivity and passive beamsplitters provide the photon interference needed for entanglement. Detectors herald entangled states and a classical processing unit coordinates the entanglement process.

FIG. 2. Energy level diagrams of commonly used 40Ca+, 88Sr+, and 138Ba+ ions that show the two-step excitation used for (a) state preparation and (b) entanglement without requiring circularly polarized light. An electric-quadrupole transition allows a change in angular momentum of |∆m|=2, such that a π-polarized excitation to the stretched state of an excited level with a dipole-allowed decay back to the ground state leaves the ion with a net change of |∆m|=1 in the pro- jection of angular momentum.

FIG. 4. Pipeline for entanglement generation separated into blocks that can execute in parallel. Pre-cooled ions from a buffer move into the entanglement zone. After a successful herald, the recoil is corrected and consecutive ion pairs are buffered and then combined for a local CNOT. The ion pair undergoes leakage checks in the detection zone before the tar- get ion is read out to determine the distilled state parity. A successfully distilled control ion exits the Bell factory while remaining ions are recycled to the starting buffer.
